title: USB drive in the parking lot
story: You find an unmarked USB drive near the office entrance. It might belong to someone, but you do not know what is on it.

actions.text: Plug it into your work laptop to identify its owner
actions.feedback: Unknown removable media can contain malicious files or attack hardware. Connecting it could expose your device or organization.

actions.text: Leave it alone and tell a coworker
actions.feedback: You avoided connecting it. Report it to the designated IT or security team so it can be handled safely.

actions.text: Do not connect it; report where you found it to IT or security
actions.feedback: This avoids the bait and gives trained staff a chance to follow the organization's media-handling procedure.

objectives: Google Cybersecurity Certificate · Assets, Threats, and Vulnerabilities

title: USB labeled Payroll on your desk
story: A small drive labeled Payroll 2026 is left beside your keyboard. Nobody on your team mentioned sharing files.

actions.text: Plug it in because the label looks important
actions.feedback: A convincing label is part of the lure. Unknown removable media can deliver malware or attack the computer directly.

actions.text: Put it in a drawer and tell your manager later
actions.feedback: You did not connect it, which avoids the immediate device risk. Report it promptly so security can follow the media procedure.

actions.text: Leave it disconnected and report its location to IT/security
actions.feedback: Do not inspect unknown media yourself. Let the designated team handle and document it.

objectives: Google Cybersecurity Certificate · assets and threats

title: Unknown phone charging at a workstation
story: A phone you do not recognize is connected to a work laptop. A device warning appeared, and the laptop is still running.

actions.text: Unlock the phone to find its owner
actions.feedback: Do not explore an unknown device or dismiss the warning. That could change evidence or expose the workstation.

actions.text: Stop using the laptop and notify the nearby IT desk
actions.feedback: Stopping work and alerting IT is safer than continuing. Follow their isolation instructions.

actions.text: Do not interact with the phone; isolate the laptop using policy and contact the security team
actions.feedback: Contain the possible connection without investigating the phone. Preserve the device state and let responders collect evidence.

title: The sick computer
story: A workstation is unusually slow, its fan is loud, and unfamiliar pop-ups appeared. A monitoring alert reports one process using 95% CPU.

actions.text: Install a cleaner from the pop-up and keep working
actions.feedback: The pop-up may be part of the problem. Installing an unapproved tool can add malware and destroy useful evidence.

actions.text: Save a note about the symptoms and ask the help desk what to do
actions.feedback: Reporting symptoms is good. Do not keep using the device if policy says to isolate it.

actions.text: Stop using it, isolate it according to policy, and report the process alert to the SOC
actions.feedback: Contain the possible compromise and preserve evidence. Responders can investigate the process safely.

title: Ransomware note
story: Files will not open. A note demands payment and gives a deadline. The computer is still connected to the office network.

actions.text: Pay immediately and delete the note
actions.feedback: Payment does not guarantee recovery and deleting the note removes evidence. Follow the incident plan.

actions.text: Take a photo of the note and contact the help desk
actions.feedback: Reporting and preserving details is helpful. Avoid continuing to use or connect the affected device.

actions.text: Isolate the device per policy, preserve the note, and contact the incident-response team
actions.feedback: Contain possible spread and preserve evidence. Responders can determine recovery from verified clean backups; do not make payment decisions yourself.

objectives: Google Cybersecurity Certificate · threats and response

title: Someone follows you through the badge door
story: A person carrying boxes walks close behind you as you badge into a restricted office. They say their hands are full and ask you to hold the door.

actions.text: Hold the secure door open because they look busy
actions.feedback: A friendly story does not verify authorization. Letting someone bypass the badge check is tailgating.

actions.text: Ask them to use their badge and point them to reception
actions.feedback: You avoided granting access. Follow the site's procedure if they refuse or the situation feels unsafe.

actions.text: Do not let them follow you in; use the visitor process and notify security
actions.feedback: Each person should authenticate at the controlled entry. The visitor process verifies identity and authorization.

title: Lost work laptop
story: You notice your assigned laptop is missing after leaving the train. It may contain work data, and you are not sure whether full-disk encryption was enabled.

actions.text: Wait a few days in case someone returns it
actions.feedback: Delay can give another person time to access data. Report loss promptly so the organization can protect accounts and data.

actions.text: Call your manager and ask whether to report it
actions.feedback: Tell your manager, but use the formal lost-device/security reporting process right away as well.

actions.text: Report it immediately through the approved channel and follow the remote lock/wipe process
actions.feedback: Fast reporting lets the organization revoke sessions, locate or lock the device, and determine whether a remote wipe is appropriate.

title: Shoulder surfer on the train
story: A passenger repeatedly watches your screen while you enter a work password on your laptop. You have not seen them touch the device.

actions.text: Confront them and show the password field
actions.feedback: Do not reveal more information or escalate the situation. Protect the screen and follow workplace reporting guidance.

actions.text: Turn away from the screen and finish later in a private place
actions.feedback: Stopping the exposure is sensible. Lock the screen before moving and report the observation if your policy requires it.

actions.text: Stop typing, lock the device, shield the screen, and change the credential if it may have been seen
actions.feedback: Reduce visual exposure, protect the session, and use the approved password process if you think the credential was observed.

title: Fake browser update
story: A full-screen page claims your browser is out of date and offers a download button. The warning appeared on a recipe site and is not part of the browser settings.

actions.text: Download and run the update from the pop-up
actions.feedback: The page may deliver unwanted software. Update through the browser's built-in settings or approved software portal.

actions.text: Close the tab and ask IT if the alert returns
actions.feedback: Closing the page avoids the download. Report repeated or unusual alerts under your organization's process.

actions.text: Do not click the pop-up; close the page and check updates through the known browser settings
actions.feedback: A webpage cannot prove it is a genuine updater. Use the application's own trusted update path.

title: Malware behavior lab
story: A fictional endpoint report says a file disguised as a free utility encrypts documents and asks for money. The report is a training sample, not a real alert.

actions.text: Classify the behavior as ransomware and follow the approved containment and recovery plan
actions.feedback: Ransomware encrypts or blocks access to data to demand payment. Contain, preserve evidence, and recover from clean backups under the incident plan.

actions.text: Classify it as spyware and delete the sample
actions.feedback: You recognized malware, but the behavior described is specifically ransomware. Do not delete evidence outside the response process.

actions.text: Run the sample on a work laptop to see what it does
actions.feedback: Never execute an unknown sample on a normal workstation. Use an isolated, authorized malware-analysis environment.
